terms.definition: Axis-aligned bounding box: a rectangle whose sides stay lined up with the x and y axes. Two AABBs overlap when they overlap on both axes, which takes only four comparisons.
Letting the editor pick the right tile variant (edge, corner, middle) automatically by looking at which neighbouring cells are filled.
A number built by adding powers of two for yes/no facts. In autotiling: up = 1, right = 2, down = 4, left = 8, giving a value from 0 to 15.
A box in the middle of the screen where the player can move without the camera following. The camera only moves when the player pushes past its edge.
The fixed set of colours an artwork or game is allowed to use. Pixel art often limits the palette so everything looks consistent.
A short grace period (often about 0.1 s) after running off a ledge when the player can still jump — named after cartoon coyotes who hang in the air before falling.
The time that passed since the last update, in seconds. Multiplying speeds by delta time makes movement the same on fast and slow computers.
The sequence in which layers are painted each frame. Things drawn later appear on top of things drawn earlier.
Updating physics in equal slices of time (such as 1/60 s) no matter how often the screen redraws, so the game behaves identically on every computer.
How many pictures are shown per second. For an animation it sets how long each drawing stays on screen; for a display it is how often the screen redraws.
How controlling a game feels moment to moment: responsiveness, weight, and the feedback that confirms every action.
The cycle a game repeats many times per second: read input, update the world, then draw it.
The invisible shape the game uses for collisions. It is often smaller than the drawing so near-misses feel fair.
Freezing the game for a few hundredths of a second at an important moment, such as a hit or a pickup, so the player notices it.
Extra feedback layered on top of game rules — particles, sound, shake, squash — that makes actions feel satisfying without changing what they do.
Remembering a jump press for a short time (often about 0.1 s) so a press just before landing still makes the character jump.
Moving a fraction of the way from one value to another. Repeating it each frame makes a camera glide smoothly toward its target.
Enlarging an image by copying each pixel into a solid block, with no blending, so pixel art stays crisp instead of blurry.
A platform you can jump up through from below but stand on from above. It only collides while the player is falling onto its top.
Showing the previous animation frame faintly behind the one you are drawing, like tracing paper, so motion between frames stays smooth.
Moving background layers slower than the foreground as the camera scrolls, which tricks the eye into seeing depth in a flat 2D game.
A brush that chooses which tile to place using a rule about its neighbours, such as grass when nothing is above and dirt underneath.
Briefly jiggling the camera by random small offsets that fade out, to make an impact or failure feel strong.
The part of a sprite sheet copied when drawing one frame, given as x, y, width and height on the sheet.
A small 2D image that a game draws and moves around as one object, such as a character, coin or bullet.
One image that holds many animation frames side by side. The game shows one frame at a time by copying its rectangle.
An animation principle: squash a shape when it lands and stretch it when it launches, keeping its volume, so motion looks springy and alive.
A system that is always in exactly one state (like idle, run or jump) and switches between states only when a rule says so.
A rule that moves a state machine from one state to another, such as fall → land when the player touches the floor.
A grid that records which tile goes in each cell. One grid can draw the level and tell the physics where walls are.
A collection of same-size square images (tiles) used to build levels, along with rules such as which tiles are solid.
A collision bug where an object moves so far in one step that it skips completely past a thin wall without ever overlapping it.
Letting the player control jump height by how long they hold the button: releasing early cuts the upward speed for a shorter hop.
